title: "Native AOT"
description: "Native AOT compiles your app to native machine code when you publish it. The published app does not use a JIT compiler and does not load the .NET runtime host. Your code, Reactor and the .NET libraries you use become one native .exe."
---

Reactor is built for this. The core library is marked AOT compatible,
it builds with zero trimming and AOT warnings, and CI runs the full selftest
suite as a Native AOT binary on every pull request. Your own code must follow
the same rules: reflection that the compiler cannot see at build time can fail
at run time, even when the build is clean.

This page shows how to turn AOT on, what Reactor does for you, how to fix
reflection in your own code, how to keep devtools in an AOT build, and how to
troubleshoot a published app.

The page is based on two small samples:
[`hello-world-aot`](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/tree/main/samples/apps/hello-world-aot)
(devtools removed) and
[`hello-world-aot-devtools-on`](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/tree/main/samples/apps/hello-world-aot-devtools-on)
(devtools kept). For the other ways to ship an app, such as MSIX and
single-file, see [Packaging](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/packaging).

## Reference [#reference]

| Setting or API | Where | What it does | When you need it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PublishAot` | Project file | Compiles the app to native code on `dotnet publish`. Also runs the trim and AOT analyzers on every build. | Always |
| `-r win-x64` / `-r win-arm64` | Publish command | Picks the target. A Native AOT publish needs a runtime identifier. | Always |
| `-p:Platform=x64` / `-p:Platform=ARM64` | Publish command | Matches the WinUI platform to the runtime identifier. | Always |
| `InvariantGlobalization` | Project file | Leaves out culture data. Numbers and dates use the invariant culture. | Optional, for size |
| `OptimizationPreference`, `StackTraceSupport`, `DebugType` | Project file | Make the `.exe` smaller. | Optional, for size |
| `IlcGenerateMstatFile` | Project file | Writes a `.mstat` file that records what the compiler kept. | Optional, for size checks |
| `Reactor.DevtoolsSupport` | `RuntimeHostConfigurationOption` | Keeps or removes the devtools code. Off by default in Release. | Only for devtools in AOT |
| `ReactorApp.RegisterAllBuiltIns()` | Startup code | Registers every built-in control handler. | Only for element records built with `new` |
| `EventSourceSupport` | Project file | Turns `EventSource` tracing back on. Native AOT turns it off by default. | Only for ETW tracing |

![Native AOT publish flow. The project file sets PublishAot. dotnet build runs the trim and AOT analyzers and reports IL2xxx and IL3xxx warnings. dotnet publish with a win-x64 or win-arm64 runtime identifier runs ILCompiler, which removes unreachable code and produces a native MyApp.exe with no JIT. The Reactor.DevtoolsSupport feature switch is a constant for ILCompiler: when it is off, the devtools code is removed and CI checks the .mstat file for this; when it is on and the Devtools package is referenced, the devtools code is kept.](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/images/native-aot/publish-flow.svg)

## Why Native AOT [#why-native-aot]

- **No JIT at run time.** The compiler turns your code into machine code
  when you publish. The app does not compile methods while it starts.
- **No runtime host.** The app does not load `coreclr.dll` or the other .NET
  host files. The repo's startup benchmark notes that a non-AOT C# app pays
  about 70–100 ms of CLR bootstrap cost compared with a pure C++ WinUI app
  ([`tests/startup_perf/README.md`](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/blob/main/tests/startup_perf/README.md)).
  The repo does not publish a measured AOT startup time for a Reactor app, so
  measure your own.
- **One native binary for your code.** Your code, Reactor and the .NET
  libraries become one `.exe`. Files that are not .NET code, such as the
  Windows App SDK bootstrapper and the app's `.pri` resource file, still ship
  next to it.
- **Only the code you use.** The compiler removes code that nothing can
  reach. CI fails if `hello-world-aot.exe` grows over 13,107,200 bytes
  (12.5 MiB)
  ([`tools/Reactor.MstatVerifier`](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/tree/main/tools/Reactor.MstatVerifier)).

The cost is that the app cannot load or generate code at run time. Code that
finds types or members by reflection only works if the compiler can see
those types and members at build time. A published app also has no
[hot reload](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/hot-reload): hot reload needs the JIT, so keep Debug builds on
JIT for the inner loop.

## Turn on Native AOT [#turn-on-native-aot]

Add `PublishAot` to the app project. This is the project shape of the repo's
AOT stress benchmark, which publishes with Native AOT in CI:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <OutputType>WinExe</OutputType>
  <TargetFramework>net10.0-windows10.0.22621.0</TargetFramework>
  <Platforms>x64;ARM64</Platforms>
  <RootNamespace>StressPerf.Reactor</RootNamespace>
  <AssemblyName>StressPerf.Reactor</AssemblyName>
  <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
  <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  <UseWinUI>true</UseWinUI>
  <WindowsPackageType>None</WindowsPackageType>
  <PublishAot>true</PublishAot>
</PropertyGroup>
```

Set `PublishAot` for every configuration, not only Release. The property only
changes `dotnet publish`, but it also turns on the trim and AOT analyzers for
every build, so you see warnings while you write code.

Publish once for each architecture:

```powershell
dotnet publish -c Release -r win-x64   -p:Platform=x64   -o out/x64
dotnet publish -c Release -r win-arm64 -p:Platform=ARM64 -o out/arm64
```

The publish step calls the MSVC linker (`link.exe`). Install the Visual
Studio C++ build tools and run the publish from a Visual Studio Developer
Command Prompt or Developer PowerShell. The repo's own AOT instructions in
[`TESTING.md`](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/blob/main/TESTING.md)
do the same.

The two samples in the repo set `PublishAot` only when you pass
`-p:PublishAotInternal=true`, so a normal build of the whole repo skips the
slow native compile. CI publishes them like this:

```powershell
dotnet publish samples/apps/hello-world-aot/HelloWorldAot.csproj -p:PublishAotInternal=true -p:Platform=x64 -r win-x64 -c Release -o out/hello-world-aot
```

Your own app does not need that property. Set `PublishAot` directly.

The program itself needs nothing special. This is the whole
`hello-world-aot` app:

```csharp
ReactorApp.Run<App>("Hello World AOT", width: 480, height: 240);

internal sealed class App : Component
{
    public override Element Render() => TextBlock("Hello, world!");
}
```

### Make the binary smaller [#make-the-binary-smaller]

The `hello-world-aot` sample adds these properties to stay under its CI size
limit. All of them are optional:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <InvariantGlobalization>true</InvariantGlobalization>
  <StackTraceSupport>false</StackTraceSupport>
  <OptimizationPreference>Size</OptimizationPreference>
  <IlcGenerateMstatFile>true</IlcGenerateMstatFile>

  <!-- No managed or native PDB files. The native PDB is about 45 MB. -->
  <DebugType>none</DebugType>
  <DebugSymbols>false</DebugSymbols>
  <NativeDebugSymbols>false</NativeDebugSymbols>
  <CopyOutputSymbolsToPublishDirectory>false</CopyOutputSymbolsToPublishDirectory>

  <!-- Don't copy .xml and .pdb files next to referenced assemblies. -->
  <AllowedReferenceRelatedFileExtensions>none</AllowedReferenceRelatedFileExtensions>
</PropertyGroup>
```

Know what each one costs:

- `InvariantGlobalization` makes number and date formatting use the
  invariant culture. Leave it off if your app formats values for the user's
  locale.
- `StackTraceSupport=false` removes method names from exception stack
  traces. Leave it on while you debug a published build.
- Without symbols you cannot debug the published `.exe` at source level.

## What Reactor does for AOT [#what-reactor-does-for-aot]

- **The core library is AOT compatible.** `Reactor.csproj` sets
  `IsAotCompatible=true`, and the repo treats trimming and AOT warnings as
  errors, so a change that adds unsafe reflection cannot merge.
- **Development code sits behind feature switches.** Devtools code is guarded
  by the `Reactor.DevtoolsSupport` switch. Release builds set it to `false`
  with `Trim="true"`, so the compiler treats it as a constant and removes the
  devtools code. CI publishes `hello-world-aot` and checks its `.mstat` file
  to prove the devtools types are gone.
- **Control families stay separate.** The core never references a specific
  control family, such as charting or docking, directly. An app that never
  draws a chart does not carry the charting code.
- **Controls register lazily.** Each factory registers its control handler
  the first time you call it. A control you never create is never
  registered, so the compiler can remove it.

### Element records built with `new` [#element-records-built-with-new]

Lazy registration has one catch. If you build an element record with `new`
instead of its factory, nothing registers its handler:

```csharp
sealed class DirectRecordApp : Component
{
    // `new` skips the TextBlock() factory, so it does not register the TextBlock handler.
    public override Element Render() => new TextBlockElement("Built without a factory");
}
```

The first mount then throws `InvalidOperationException` with the message
*No handler is registered for element type …*. This happens in JIT builds
too; it is not specific to AOT. There are two common fixes. Call the
factory once before the first mount. This registers only that control:

```csharp
// Registers only the TextBlock handler. Other controls stay trimmable.
_ = TextBlock("");
ReactorApp.Run<DirectRecordApp>("Direct records", width: 480, height: 240);
```

Or register the whole built-in catalog at startup:

```csharp
// Registers every built-in control handler. The trimmer then keeps all of them.
ReactorApp.RegisterAllBuiltIns();
ReactorApp.Run<DirectRecordApp>("Direct records", width: 480, height: 240);
```

`ReactorApp.RegisterAllBuiltIns()` is safe to call more than once and
applies to the whole process. It is an ordinary method, so an app that never
calls it pays nothing. An app that calls it keeps every built-in control
handler in the binary, even the ones it never uses. That is why AOT apps that
only use factories should not call it. The repo's AOT trim test app
([`tests/aot_trim_proof/Reactor.AotHelloWorld`](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/tree/main/tests/aot_trim_proof/Reactor.AotHelloWorld))
never calls it.

Use it when much of your code builds records with `new`, for example a hot
loop that skips factories (see [Hot loops](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/advanced#hot-loops)). For your
own or third-party controls, register them with
`ControlRegistry.Register<TElement, TControl>` instead; see
[Extending Reactor controls](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/extending-reactor-controls). Elements
generated with `[GenerateReactorWrapper]` register from their static
constructor, so creating one is enough.

## What works and what doesn't [#what-works-and-what-doesnt]

Most of Reactor works under Native AOT: the reconciler, factories and
modifiers, hooks, flex layout, theming, animation, commanding, Markdown,
charting, the built-in WinUI controls, generated localization, and
unpackaged jump lists.

A few features use reflection that the compiler cannot follow. They build
without warnings, because the library suppresses the warnings, but they fail
at run time in an AOT app:

| Feature | Use instead |
|---|---|
| `AutoColumns<T>` for a [data grid](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/data-system) | Explicit `Column<T>(...)` columns |
| `UseObservableTree` on plain objects | `Observable<T>` or an observable collection |
| PropertyGrid auto-discovery and its array editor | Register editors by hand, or use a JIT build |
| `FormField(field, value, onChange)`, which picks the editor from a `FieldDescriptor` | `FormField(content, label: ...)` with an editor you choose |
| Devtools DP discovery (`properties`, `setProperty`) | Inspect a JIT build |
| `{TemplateBinding}` to private DPs in a third-party assembly with no `.xaml` file | `ReactorApp.RegisterControlAssembly(provider)` |

The full list, with issue links, is in
[`docs/aot-support.md`](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/blob/main/docs/aot-support.md).

## Reflection in your own code [#reflection-in-your-own-code]

The compiler keeps only the code and metadata it can see. Three patterns
cause most problems in app code. Each comment shows the warning the analyzer
reports.

### Types found by name [#types-found-by-name]

```csharp
// Avoid: the type name is only known at run time.
var type = Type.GetType(pageTypeName);   // IL2057
var page = Activator.CreateInstance(type!);
```

The compiler cannot know which type the string names, so it may remove the
type. Name each type in code instead. A dictionary of factories keeps exactly
the pages it lists:

```csharp
sealed class HomePage : Component
{
    public override Element Render() => TextBlock("Home");
}

sealed class SettingsPage : Component
{
    public override Element Render() => TextBlock("Settings");
}

static class Pages
{
    // Each entry names its type in code, so the trimmer keeps exactly these pages.
    static readonly Dictionary<string, Func<Element>> ByName = new()
    {
        ["home"] = () => Component<HomePage>(),
        ["settings"] = () => Component<SettingsPage>(),
    };

    public static Element Create(string name) =>
        ByName.TryGetValue(name, out var create) ? create() : TextBlock($"Unknown page: {name}");
}
```

### JSON without a source generator [#json-without-a-source-generator]

```csharp
// Avoid: reflection-based serialization.
var json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(settings);   // IL2026 and IL3050
```

Reflection-based `System.Text.Json` reads properties at run time and may
generate code. Use a `JsonSerializerContext`. The source generator writes the
serializer at build time:

```csharp
record AppSettings(string Theme, int FontSize);

// The source generator writes the serializer at build time, so no reflection runs.
[JsonSerializable(typeof(AppSettings))]
partial class SettingsJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext { }

static class SettingsStore
{
    public static string Save(AppSettings settings) =>
        JsonSerializer.Serialize(settings, SettingsJsonContext.Default.AppSettings);

    public static AppSettings? Load(string json) =>
        JsonSerializer.Deserialize(json, SettingsJsonContext.Default.AppSettings);
}
```

### Members of a generic type [#members-of-a-generic-type]

```csharp
// Avoid: T has no annotation, so the compiler may remove its properties.
static IEnumerable<string> Names<T>() =>
    typeof(T).GetProperties().Select(p => p.Name);   // IL2090
```

Tell the compiler which members to keep with `[DynamicallyAccessedMembers]`.
The annotation flows to every caller, so each type passed as `T` keeps its
public properties:

```csharp
static class PropertyNames
{
    // The annotation tells the trimmer to keep T's public properties
    // for every type that callers pass in.
    public static IEnumerable<string> Of<
        [DynamicallyAccessedMembers(DynamicallyAccessedMemberTypes.PublicProperties)] T>() =>
        typeof(T).GetProperties().Select(p => p.Name);
}
```

## Read trimming and AOT warnings [#read-trimming-and-aot-warnings]

Warnings that start with `IL2` come from the trim analyzer. Warnings that
start with `IL3` come from the AOT analyzer. Each one names a call that may
fail after trimming or AOT compilation. The ones you see most often:

| Warning | Meaning | Usual fix |
|---|---|---|
| `IL2026` | The call has `[RequiresUnreferencedCode]`: it needs code the trimmer may remove. | Use a trim-safe API, such as a source generator. |
| `IL3050` | The call has `[RequiresDynamicCode]`: it generates code at run time. | Use a trim-safe API, such as a source generator. |
| `IL2057` | `Type.GetType` gets a string the compiler cannot read. | Name the type in code. |
| `IL2070`, `IL2090` | Reflection on a `Type` or `T` that has no `[DynamicallyAccessedMembers]` annotation. | Add the annotation. |
| `IL3000` | `Assembly.Location` is empty in a single-file or AOT app. | Use `AppContext.BaseDirectory`. |
| `IL2104`, `IL3053` | A package produced warnings. They are folded into one warning per assembly. | Set `<TrimmerSingleWarn>false</TrimmerSingleWarn>` to see each one. |

Work through warnings in this order:

1. Remove the reflection. Name types in code, or use a source generator.
2. If you need reflection, annotate it with `[DynamicallyAccessedMembers]` so
   the compiler keeps the members.
3. If neither works, mark your own method with `[RequiresUnreferencedCode]`
   or `[RequiresDynamicCode]`. The warning then moves to your callers, where
   someone can decide.

Do not silence a warning with `[UnconditionalSuppressMessage]` unless you
have proved the code is safe. A suppressed warning still fails at run time.

## Devtools in AOT builds [#devtools-in-aot-builds]

By default a Release build has no devtools. The `Reactor.DevtoolsSupport`
switch is off, the compiler removes the devtools code, and the
`Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Devtools` package is not referenced. This is what you
want for a shipped app.

Devtools in an AOT build need three things:

1. The `Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Devtools` package.
2. The `Reactor.DevtoolsSupport` switch set to `true`.
3. A `--devtools` argument when the app starts, for example `--devtools run`.

The project file of `hello-world-aot-devtools-on` adds the first two:

```xml
<ItemGroup>
  <RuntimeHostConfigurationOption Include="Reactor.DevtoolsSupport" Value="true" Trim="true" />
</ItemGroup>

<ItemGroup>
  <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Devtools" Version="0.1.0-preview.18" />
</ItemGroup>
```

Its `Program.cs` also calls `ReactorDevtools.EnsureRegistered()`. Reactor
loads the devtools assembly by name, which the compiler cannot follow. The
direct call gives the compiler a reference, so it keeps the devtools
assembly:

```csharp
// Program.cs of an app that keeps devtools in its AOT build.
ReactorDevtools.EnsureRegistered();
ReactorApp.Run<App>("Hello World AOT Devtools On", width: 480, height: 240);
```

Set the switch in the project file, not with `AppContext.SetSwitch` in code.
An AOT build replaces the switch with the project file value at compile time,
so a call at run time has no effect.

To turn the switch on for one build without editing the project, pass
`-p:ReactorDiagnostics=true`. It also turns on source maps.
`Reactor.targets` warns not to ship a build made with it. You still need the
Devtools package for `--devtools`.

If an app built without devtools gets `--devtools run`, it does not open a
normal window. It writes this to standard error and exits with code 2:

```text
[reactor] --devtools requested but this binary was built without Reactor.DevtoolsSupport or without the Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Devtools package. Devtools must be enabled at build time. Add the following to your csproj and rebuild:
  <RuntimeHostConfigurationOption Include="Reactor.DevtoolsSupport" Value="true" Trim="true" />
```

Some devtools features do less under AOT. DP discovery for `properties` and
`setProperty` returns empty results, and the tool adds a notice that says
why. For day-to-day work, use devtools in a Debug (JIT) build. Build an AOT
devtools binary only to look at a problem that only happens under AOT. See
[Devtools](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/devtools) for how to use devtools.

## Tracing in AOT builds [#tracing-in-aot-builds]

Native AOT turns `EventSourceSupport` off by default, which removes all
`EventSource` code. A published app then sends no Reactor ETW events, not
even warnings. To trace an AOT build, opt back in:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <EventSourceSupport>true</EventSourceSupport>
</PropertyGroup>
```

See [Diagnostics](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/diagnostics) and
[Perf instrumentation](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/how-it-works/perf-instrumentation) for the events and how to
capture them.

## Troubleshooting [#troubleshooting]

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| The publish fails at the link step, or `link.exe` is not found. | The MSVC linker is not on the path. | Install the Visual Studio C++ build tools and publish from a Developer Command Prompt. |
| The published app crashes at startup or cannot load its XAML. | The `.pri` resource file is missing from the publish output. Older Reactor previews did not copy it. | Update Reactor. The "Publish output" section of [`docs/aot-support.md`](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/blob/main/docs/aot-support.md) has a fix for older versions. |
| `InvalidOperationException`: *No handler is registered for element type …* | An element record was built with `new` before anything registered its handler. | Call the factory once, register the control, or call `ReactorApp.RegisterAllBuiltIns()`. See [Element records built with `new`](#element-records-built-with-new). |
| The process exits with code `0xC0000409`. | An unhandled managed exception. Native AOT ends the process with a fast fail. | Capture a dump, as described in `docs/aot-support.md`. Keep `StackTraceSupport` on while you debug. |
| A feature works in a JIT build but not in the AOT build, with no warning. | Reflection behind a suppressed warning. | Check the table in [What works and what doesn't](#what-works-and-what-doesnt). |
| A third-party control's template is broken. | Its assembly has no registered `IXamlMetadataProvider`. | Call `ReactorApp.RegisterControlAssembly(provider)` at startup. |
| `--devtools run` prints a message and exits with code 2. | The switch is off or the Devtools package is missing. | Add both, as in [Devtools in AOT builds](#devtools-in-aot-builds). |
| A trace of the published app has no Reactor events. | `EventSourceSupport` is off. | Set `<EventSourceSupport>true</EventSourceSupport>`. |

A bug that goes away when you add a diagnostic `typeof(T).GetProperties()`
call is still a bug. That call makes the compiler keep the metadata the app
was missing, so it hides the problem. Delete the probe and check again.

> **Caveat:** A clean build does not prove that an AOT app works. Several Reactor features
> suppress their trim warnings but still use reflection, and they fail at run
> time under `PublishAot=true`: `AutoColumns<T>`, `UseObservableTree` on plain
> objects, PropertyGrid auto-discovery and the `FieldDescriptor` overload of
> `FormField`. Suggest
> explicit columns and explicit observables instead. Do not suggest
> `ReactorApp.RegisterAllBuiltIns()` for an app that only uses factories,
> because it keeps every built-in control in the binary. Devtools are off in
> Release builds by default; an AOT build with devtools needs the
> `Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Devtools` package, the `Reactor.DevtoolsSupport` switch
> and a `--devtools` argument. Native AOT has no hot reload, and it emits no
> ETW events unless `EventSourceSupport` is `true`.

## Patterns [#patterns]

### Set PublishAot from the first day [#set-publishaot-from-the-first-day]

Turn on `PublishAot` when you create the project, even if you ship with JIT
at first. The analyzers then flag reflection while the code is still small
and easy to change.

### Test the published binary [#test-the-published-binary]

Run the published `.exe` in CI, not only the build. Reactor's CI publishes
the selftest host with Native AOT and runs the whole suite against it,
because a warning-free build can still fail at run time.

### Name types in code [#name-types-in-code]

Replace lookups by string with code that names each type, such as the
[page registry](#types-found-by-name) above. The compiler then keeps exactly
the types the app uses.

### Keep a separate devtools build [#keep-a-separate-devtools-build]

Ship a build with devtools removed, and keep a second build or project with
devtools on for debugging AOT-only problems. The two `hello-world-aot`
samples show this split.

## Common Mistakes [#common-mistakes]

### Trusting a clean build [#trusting-a-clean-build]

The library suppresses warnings for features it knows use reflection, so the
build of an app that uses `AutoColumns<T>` is clean. The app still fails at
run time. Check [the list](#what-works-and-what-doesnt) and run the
published binary.

### Building records with `new` and no registration [#building-records-with-new-and-no-registration]

A component that returns `new ButtonElement(...)` before any `Button(...)`
call throws on first mount. Call the factory once or register the control,
as in [Element records built with `new`](#element-records-built-with-new).

### Calling RegisterAllBuiltIns by habit [#calling-registerallbuiltins-by-habit]

`ReactorApp.RegisterAllBuiltIns()` keeps every built-in control handler in
the binary. An app that only uses factories does not need it and gets
bigger for no benefit.

### Using InvariantGlobalization in a localized app [#using-invariantglobalization-in-a-localized-app]

`InvariantGlobalization` saves space, but numbers and dates then use the
invariant culture for every user. Leave it off if the app shows formatted
values. See [Localization](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/localization).

### Shipping a diagnostics build [#shipping-a-diagnostics-build]

A build made with `-p:ReactorDiagnostics=true` keeps devtools publishing
code and source maps. Use it to debug, and never ship it.

## Tips [#tips]

**Publish early.** An AOT publish is much slower than a normal build. The
repo's selftest host takes 10–15 minutes. Publish a small app first, then
add features, so you find problems one at a time.

**Keep the inner loop on JIT.** Debug builds run with the JIT, so
[hot reload](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/tools/hot-reload) and full devtools keep working. Publish with AOT
to test and ship.

**Check what the compiler kept.** With `IlcGenerateMstatFile` set, the
publish writes a `.mstat` file next to the intermediate build output. The
repo's CI reads it with
[`tools/Reactor.MstatVerifier`](https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-reactor/tree/main/tools/Reactor.MstatVerifier)
to prove that devtools types are absent.

**Leave optional packages out.** Reference `Microsoft.UI.Reactor.Advanced`
only if you use its controls. It adds [Win2D](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/controls/win2d-canvas) to the publish output. See
[Packaging](/microsoft-ui-reactor/main/guides/packaging).
